title: 2027-06-21 Threshold variance surgery and safety transfer
next_steps: Redwood to run controlled benchmark with historical traffic replay and share results (Sofia, due 2027-06-25)
Customer to provide 3 sample failing request traces and retention window details (Maya, due 2027-06-23)
Schedule follow-up canary test session with infra+SEs (tentative 2027-06-28)
Exchange SOC2/ISO evidence and KMS integration notes (Oliver to confirm by 2027-06-24)
action_items: Marcus (Redwood SE): prepare batch/quantization experiment matrix and run initial sims; deliver CSV + notes by 2027-06-25
Sofia (AE): send updated pricing estimate for Dedicated pool + burst buffer by 2027-06-22
Maya (Crescent SRE): export 3 longest tail request traces and upload to secure share by 2027-06-23
Oliver (Crescent Sec): confirm KMS/HSM key policy and share diagram by 2027-06-24
Elena (CSM): create follow-up invite for canary test and include runbook link by 2027-06-22
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): okay everyone, thanks for joining. Uh this is the threshold variance surgery and safety transfer, um the goal is to go through the root cause we saw last week and hand off the containment and rollback runbook. Recording now.
[00:22] Jared (Crescent VP Eng): thanks. Quick note — we got quite a lot of exec pressure; the latency spikes caused a visible downstream error to our user billing workflow so we need an action plan.
[00:34] Maya (Crescent SRE): yeah, and to be clear, it's not constant — it's these high percentile surges when concurrent sessions hit a certain token window, the queue backs up and then eviction happens.
[00:48] Marcus (Redwood SE): right, thanks Maya. I reviewed the traces you uploaded last night, and there are two things that jumped out — the max-sequence paths that bypassed prefix cache, and a burst of large embedding requests that caused compaction churn on the K V cache — sometimes transcribed as K-V cash in the logs.
[01:10] Oliver (Crescent Sec): just to flag security constraints — we cannot ship any runbook that requires moving PII out of the VPC. Any mitigations need to work with our KMS policy and audit logging.
[01:22] Sofia (Redwood AE): understood. We'll scope mitigations that fit the private deployment constraints. Marcus, can you go deep on what you found?
[01:30] Marcus (Redwood SE): yeah. So, baseline: you're on Redwood Dedicated with a 4-GPU pool, pinned to the rtx-like family, um the interesting part is the sequence-length distribution. Normally avg length is 120 tokens, but a small subset of customer flows spike to 2k tokens. When those hit, the runtime's dynamic batching tries to fold requests, and the KV ram pressure grows — we saw eviction thresholds trigger and then token-level latency jumps.
[02:05] Maya (Crescent SRE): we saw latency go from 120ms p50 to multi-second p99s and then timeouts. The first sign was increased queue depth in our frontend.
[02:18] Marcus (Redwood SE): exactly. There are a couple of levers: 1) tighten dynamic batching max-window for that route, 2) enable prefix/KV caching for templates used by those flows, 3) fallback to a smaller model variant when token length > threshold, or 4) provision burst capacity. Each has tradeoffs.
[02:42] Jared (Crescent VP Eng): what's the fastest to implement? We need a near-term containment we can run in less than a day.
[02:49] Marcus (Redwood SE): fastest is config-level — reduce max batch depth for that route and set a token-length cutoff so very long requests go to a dedicated queue with tighter concurrency. That is a config change and a routing policy update, low-risk.
[03:04] Sofia (Redwood AE): and that can be done without moving data or changing keys?
[03:08] Marcus (Redwood SE): yes, it's purely inference routing; no data egress.
[03:12] Oliver (Crescent Sec): good. We'll want the exact audit trail for that change and an ACL note.
[03:18] Marcus (Redwood SE): Redwood Console will emit the change event and we can snapshot the route policy; we also have the change ID.
[03:24] Maya (Crescent SRE): next, long-term we need to avoid the eviction spiral. What's the compute tradeoff for fallback model vs burst GPUs?
[03:33] Marcus (Redwood SE): fallback model — smaller model variant — saves RAM and KV pressure but may increase token cost due to more retries if relevance drops. Burst GPUs increase throughput but cost more and may be constrained by quota. We also have quantized profiles which reduce memory footprint but need validation for accuracy on your prompts.
[03:54] Jared (Crescent VP Eng): can you quantify — ballpark numbers?
[03:58] Marcus (Redwood SE): rough: moving to an 8-bit quantized variant can cut KV memory by ~40% on our tests; fallback to a smaller 13B model reduces peak RAM by ~60% but increases latency for some examples by ~10-15%. Burst capacity provisioning is linear cost increase — roughly 2x cost for 2x GPUs on the pool. I'll send the experiment matrix.
[04:25] Nina (Product): can we lean on caching more? A lot of these are semi-deterministic templates.
[04:30] Marcus (Redwood SE): yes, prefix caching would be high-leverage — for templated flows we can cache the KV prefix; that avoids recomputing attention states. But the cache hit rate depends on prompt normalization and we saw some variability in user-generated text that reduces hits.
[04:52] Maya (Crescent SRE): about the traces — we extracted three representative high-latency traces, but there are more. We'll upload retention windows for the last 30 days.
[05:02] Sofia (Redwood AE): thanks. Oliver — on the KMS/HSM constraint, what can you share so we can map options?
[05:09] Oliver (Crescent Sec): we use an internal HSM with strict key rotation. Any integration has to go through our key-access team and must have audit forwarding to Splunk. Also no external replication of raw logs.
[05:22] Marcus (Redwood SE): fine — our Private deployment can be configured to use your KMS endpoint and forward audit logs; we just need the endpoint and policy.
[05:32] Oliver (Crescent Sec): I'll share the diagram.
[05:35] Sofia (Redwood AE): okay, let's walk through a proposed short-term runbook — Marcus?
[05:40] Marcus (Redwood SE): short-term containment runbook (high-level): 1) Apply route threshold: set token cutoff at 1,000 for the affected route and move over-length requests to the isolated queue, 2) Reduce max batch size from 32 to 8 for that queue, 3) Enable conservative caching TTL for the template prefixes, 4) Schedule a temporary Dedicated burst node pool for 24 hours under monitoring, 5) Rollback steps: revert policy and clear isolated queue then flush cache. The rollback should be automated as a canary if errors rise.
[06:20] Maya (Crescent SRE): how do we detect when the policy should be reverted? Do you have a single signal?
[06:26] Marcus (Redwood SE): signal is a composite: p99 latency below 500ms for 10 minutes, queue depth <5, and successful request ratio > 99.5%. We can bake that into an alert.
[06:40] Jared (Crescent VP Eng): timeline to implement the config-only containment?
[06:44] Marcus (Redwood SE): plan: test in staging today, push to canary in your pre-prod tomorrow, and if green, full prod within 24 hours. So earliest containment in ~30 hours.
[06:57] Sofia (Redwood AE): good. For customers, we'll also provide a cost estimate for burst and fallback options. Marcus, can you draft that and Sofia will package it with pricing?
[07:07] Marcus (Redwood SE): yes. I'll include quantization validation notes — we should run your sample prompts through quantized models to check regressions.
[07:17] Nina (Product): what about longer-term reliability improvements?
[07:21] Marcus (Redwood SE): longer-term: 1) model routing by sequence-length binning, 2) proactive KV cache warming for heavy templates, 3) adaptive autoscaling with pre-warming for predicted spike windows, 4) evaluation harness to detect quality regressions on quantized variants, and 5) a dedicated runbook for long-tail eviction detection.
[07:44] Oliver (Crescent Sec): on the audit side we need a pre-approved freeze window if you plan any config drift that could expose data.
[07:52] Sofia (Redwood AE): we'll align to a maintenance window for any disruptive changes.
[07:57] Maya (Crescent SRE): can we see the test harness? We want to replay synthetic traffic that mirrors production.
[08:03] Marcus (Redwood SE): yes — we have a traffic replay tool. We'll run a controlled replay with your subset of traces behind your VPC connector so no logs leave your environment. You can validate the behaviour.
[08:18] Jared (Crescent VP Eng): good. A couple of customers asked about SLA credits and whether this counts as an incident in our contract — can we get a definitive classification after containment?
[08:28] Elena (Redwood CSM): we'll coordinate with support; if it's a platform regression we'll treat per the SLA. We'll produce an incident summary and classification once the RCA is complete.
[08:39] Sofia (Redwood AE): ok let's capture immediate next steps — Marcus will run experiments and Sofia will send pricing and the Deferred docs.
[08:47] Marcus (Redwood SE): just to note — in the traces, some hostnames were anonymized and the transcription shows odd word swaps — e g 'queue' became 'cue' in places — apologies if that shows up in the runbook.
[08:59] Maya (Crescent SRE): haha yes the auto transcription does weird stuff.
[09:04] Jared (Crescent VP Eng): any blockers from Redwood side?
[09:08] Marcus (Redwood SE): only needing your sample traces and the KMS endpoint for private tests. Also confirm whether you want us to run quantization validation against your golden prompt set.
[09:19] Nina (Product): yes we'll provide a golden prompt set — maybe 200 samples — but we need to scrub PII first.
[09:26] Oliver (Crescent Sec): we'll coordinate scrub. Also, please add Splunk forwarding as part of the audit handoff.
[09:33] Marcus (Redwood SE): noted.
[09:36] Sofia (Redwood AE): final recap here — containment plan starts with route policy changes (token cutoff + reduced batch depth), run controlled replay, run quant/ fallback experiments, provide cost options for burst vs fallback, and deliver a rollback/playbook. We'll reconvene after Marcus shares the experiment CSV and staging run results.
[09:56] Jared (Crescent VP Eng): sounds good. Thanks all.
[10:01] Sofia (Redwood AE): thanks, I'll send meeting notes and the action items. End call.
notes: Shared artifacts: runbook draft v1 (link: https://redwood.app/runbooks/cht-threshold-v1), experiment-matrix spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.app/sheets/cht-experiments), staging replay bucket (private link provided to customer).
closing_summary: Short-term containment: routing policy + reduced batch; Mid-term: quantization validation and fallback model; Long-term: adaptive autoscale and KV cache warming. Hand-off items: traces, KMS diagram, canary test scheduling.
